top_choice_rationale: P004 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) rests on two separable, mature programmes: electoral rules and constitutions linked to fiscal outcomes through explicit political incentives, and the political economy of state capacity. Each comes from a long partnership, so attribution is traceable. The citation can rest on the formal framework and later sharper designs rather than on cross-country regressions alone. The 2024 institutions prize concerned long-run colonial origins of prosperity, so I read the overlap as partial. Identification of constitutional effects is partly observational, and Besley is the most contestable name, so a Persson-Tabellini pair would also be defensible. P003 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) is the strongest competitor, with the most checkable identification but a task-framework credit gap outside the ballot and debated magnitudes. P002 follows, with clear originating building blocks but eight credited names and an unsettled originators-versus-estimation question. P001 ranks fourth: the credit line is clean, but the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum lineage is uncredited and the welfare magnitudes depend on functional form. A prize on any of these four is preferable to no award.
recusal_note: My spouse, Magdalena Andersson, is a party leader and former prime minister; this is a public fact with no apparent bearing on my assessment, but I disclose it because P004 is a political-economy topic. I co-authored a 2026 IJIO paper with chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen, and Hassler also prefers B016, so our agreement is not independent corroboration. My profile shows no co-authorship or institutional tie to Persson, Tabellini or Besley, nor to the credited names on P001, P002 or P003. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
